\section{Introduction}

A recurring and seductive claim holds that human mathematical intuition, or a
sufficiently powerful prediction machine, must transcend computation---that
answering arbitrary questions correctly is a noncomputable feat. The claim is
often illustrated with a fixed-length setup: statements are strings of bounded
length over a finite alphabet, and a machine is asked to judge each one true or
false with high accuracy.

The purpose of this paper is to isolate exactly what is and is not true in such
a setup, with all claims stated so precisely that each is either a theorem or a
refuted conjecture. Our central observation is deflationary: on a bounded
language the perfect oracle always exists, because the domain is finite and an
exact answer table can be written down. The motivating noncomputability claim,
taken literally for a fixed length bound, is therefore false.

Deflation is not the end of the story. The same finiteness that makes the
pointwise oracle trivial makes the \emph{uniform} oracle impossible, and the
genuinely infinitary content of Cantor's diagonal argument survives untouched.
The contribution of this paper is to lay these facts side by side as a single
hierarchy and to name, at each step, the exact modelling distinction that
governs the outcome:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
  \item \textbf{Finite domain versus practical feasibility.} A truth table can
    be astronomically large yet computable; complexity, storage, learnability,
    and computability are distinct notions.
  \item \textbf{Semantic truth versus provability.} For bounded strings a fixed
    external truth assignment has a finite table; for all arithmetic sentences,
    truth and theoremhood lead to genuinely unbounded questions.
  \item \textbf{Pointwise versus uniform accuracy.} A good oracle for one fixed
    semantics is compatible with the nonexistence of one predictor that works
    for every semantics.
  \item \textbf{Scoring of abstention.} We count ``unknown'' as incorrect;
    alternative scoring rules must be stated explicitly and may change finite
    accuracy bounds, though not the finite-table counterexample.
  \item \textbf{Counting versus diagonalization.} Counting finite functions
    yields only exponential cardinalities; noncomputability requires an
    unbounded effective presentation together with a diagonal or reduction
    argument.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The bounded language of statements}

We model statements as fixed-length words over a finite alphabet, following the
familiar ``Library of Babel'' picture in which all strings of a bounded length
form a single finite space.

\begin{definition}[Statement space]
Fix natural numbers $a$ (the \emph{alphabet size}) and $\ell$ (the
\emph{length}). A \emph{statement} is a word of length $\ell$ over an alphabet
of $a$ symbols. Write $\Stmt_{a,\ell}$ for the set of all such statements.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Cardinality of the statement space]
The statement space is finite, with
\[
  \lvert \Stmt_{a,\ell} \rvert = a^{\ell}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A word of length $\ell$ is a function from an $\ell$-element index set to an
$a$-element alphabet; the number of such functions is $a^{\ell}$. In particular
the space is finite for all $a,\ell$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Answers]
An \emph{answer} is one of $\yes$, $\no$, or $\unknown$. The map $\beta$ from
Booleans to definite answers sends $\true \mapsto \yes$ and $\false \mapsto
\no$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Semantics and oracle]
A \emph{semantics} on a set $X$ is a function $\tau : X \to \{\true,\false\}$.
An \emph{oracle} on $X$ is a function $\omega : X \to \{\yes,\no,\unknown\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Correctness and accuracy]
An oracle $\omega$ is \emph{correct} on $x$ under $\tau$ if $\omega(x) =
\beta(\tau(x))$; abstention is never correct. For finite $X$, the
\emph{correct count} is
\[
  \Correct(\tau,\omega) = \bigl\lvert \{ x \in X : \omega(x) = \beta(\tau(x)) \} \bigr\rvert,
\]
and $\omega$ \emph{meets the $95\%$ benchmark} under $\tau$ when
$95 \cdot \lvert X \rvert \le 100 \cdot \Correct(\tau,\omega)$.
\end{definition}

We use the integer form $95\lvert X\rvert \le 100\,\Correct$ to keep the
condition purely arithmetical; it is equivalent to
$\Correct/\lvert X\rvert \ge 0.95$.

\section{Pointwise existence: the perfect finite oracle}

\begin{definition}[Exact oracle]
Given a semantics $\tau$, the \emph{exact oracle} is
$\varepsilon_\tau(x) = \beta(\tau(x))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Pointwise exactness]
For every semantics $\tau$ and every $x$, the exact oracle is correct on $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By definition $\varepsilon_\tau(x) = \beta(\tau(x))$, which is the correctness
condition.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Total correctness on a finite domain]
For finite $X$ and any semantics $\tau$, $\Correct(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau) =
\lvert X \rvert$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The correctness predicate holds for every $x \in X$, so the filtered subset is
all of $X$, of cardinality $\lvert X \rvert$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect Finite Oracle]
For any finite bounded language $\Stmt_{a,\ell}$ and any semantics $\tau$, there
exists an oracle meeting the $95\%$ benchmark. In fact the exact oracle is
correct on every statement, so
$95 \cdot a^{\ell} \le 100 \cdot \Correct(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $\omega = \varepsilon_\tau$. Then $\Correct(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau) =
\lvert \Stmt_{a,\ell}\rvert = a^{\ell}$, so the benchmark reads $95 a^{\ell} \le
100 a^{\ell}$, which holds.
\end{proof}

This refutes, for a fixed length bound, the claim that a highly accurate truth
oracle cannot exist. The oracle is in fact perfectly accurate; $95\%$ could be
replaced by $100\%$.

\begin{theorem}[Finite tabulation]
Every oracle $\omega$ on a finite bounded language is completely described by a
finite list of $(\text{statement},\text{answer})$ pairs: there is a finite table
$T$ such that $(x,\omega(x)) \in T$ for every statement $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Enumerate the finitely many statements and map each to $(x,\omega(x))$. The
resulting finite list contains $(x,\omega(x))$ for every $x$ by construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Existence is not feasibility]
The oracle \emph{is} a finite object, but its size is $a^{\ell}$ rows. For
$a=26$, $\ell=100$ this exceeds $10^{141}$, far beyond any physical storage.
Computability of a finite function is automatic; tractability is a separate
question that finiteness does not address.
\end{remark}

\section{Uniform impossibility: the adversarial semantics}

\begin{definition}[Adversarial semantics]
Given an oracle $\omega$ on $X$, the \emph{adversarial semantics}
$\alpha_\omega$ falsifies each answer:
\[
  \alpha_\omega(x) =
  \begin{cases}
    \false & \omega(x) = \yes,\\
    \true & \omega(x) = \no,\\
    \true & \omega(x) = \unknown.
  \end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Pointwise adversarial failure]
For every oracle $\omega$ and every $x$, $\omega$ is incorrect on $x$ under
$\alpha_\omega$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Case on $\omega(x)$. If $\omega(x) = \yes$ then $\beta(\alpha_\omega(x)) = \no
\neq \yes$; if $\omega(x) = \no$ then $\beta(\alpha_\omega(x)) = \yes \neq \no$;
if $\omega(x) = \unknown$ then $\omega(x)$ is not a definite answer, so it cannot
equal $\beta(\alpha_\omega(x))$. Correctness fails in every case.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No Universal Oracle]
Let $X$ be a nonempty finite set. Then there is no oracle $\omega$ with
$95 \cdot \lvert X \rvert \le 100 \cdot \Correct(\tau,\omega)$ for all $\tau$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose such $\omega$ existed and apply the hypothesis with $\tau =
\alpha_\omega$. By the previous lemma $\omega$ is incorrect everywhere, so
$\Correct(\alpha_\omega,\omega) = 0$, and the benchmark demands
$95\lvert X\rvert \le 0$, contradicting $\lvert X\rvert > 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Quantifier order]
The two theorems are compatible: ``for each $\tau$ there is a good $\omega$'' is
true, while ``there is a $\omega$ good for every $\tau$'' is false. They differ
only in the order of $\forall\tau$ and $\exists\omega$. Because abstention is
scored as incorrect, even the constant $\unknown$ oracle scores zero against
$\alpha_\omega$, so hedging cannot rescue uniformity.
\end{remark}

\section{Diagonalization: finite echo and infinite force}

\subsection{The finite diagonal is counting}

\begin{definition}[Finite diagonal]
For an $n\times n$ Boolean table $R$ with rows $R_i = R(i,\cdot)$, the
\emph{finite diagonal} is $D(i) = \lnot R(i,i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Finite diagonal escape]
For any $n\times n$ Boolean table $R$ and any row index $i$, $D \neq R_i$.
Consequently the $n$ rows cannot realize all $2^n$ Boolean patterns: the map
$i \mapsto R_i$ is not surjective, including at $n=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $D = R_i$, evaluating at $i$ gives $\lnot R(i,i) = R(i,i)$, impossible. Hence
$D$ differs from every row and is omitted by the enumeration.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Only counting]
This has no computational content: it is $n < 2^n$ in disguise, an inequality
between finite cardinalities.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The infinite diagonal escapes every enumeration}

\begin{definition}[Diagonal jump]
For a table $R : \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} \to \{\true,\false\}$ with rows
$R_k = R(k,\cdot)$, the \emph{diagonal jump} is $J(k) = \lnot R(k,k)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Diagonal escape]
For any indexed family $(R_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of Boolean sequences and any $k$,
$J \neq R_k$. Therefore no countable list of Boolean sequences contains every
Boolean sequence: the family is not surjective onto the space of Boolean
sequences.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $J = R_k$, evaluate at $k$ to obtain $\lnot R(k,k) = R(k,k)$, a
contradiction. Thus $J$ lies outside the family.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the jump does and does not capture]
This captures the structural core of jump constructions---a uniformly defined
object that diagonalizes out of any indexed family---but it is deliberately not
a formalization of the Turing jump: no machine model, halting problem, or
relativized computation is invoked. Bridging the gap to computability theory
requires an effective presentation of the family plus a reduction.
\end{remark}

\section{Discussion}

Collecting the results yields a graded picture, each rung governed by a single
modelling choice:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Rung 1.} Fix a semantics, bound the length: a perfect oracle
    exists and is a finite table. Existence is free; feasibility is not
    addressed.
  \item \textbf{Rung 2.} Demand one oracle for all semantics: impossible on any
    nonempty finite domain, by quantifier order and the scoring of abstention.
  \item \textbf{Rung 3.} Diagonalize a finite square table: escape holds, but as
    a counting fact ($n < 2^n$) with no computational force.
  \item \textbf{Rung 4.} Diagonalize an infinite family: escape holds with full
    force; no countable enumeration of Boolean sequences is complete.
\end{itemize}
Under precise statement, the informal claim ``a highly accurate universal truth
oracle cannot exist'' fragments into one true existence theorem, one true
uniform impossibility, one true counting fact, and one true infinitary
escape---none of which is the sweeping noncomputability claim originally
advertised.

\emph{Auditing accuracy claims.} Any assertion that a predictor is ``$p\%$
accurate'' is incomplete without a specified finite benchmark or probability
measure and a scoring rule for abstention. Rung 1 shows $100\%$ is attainable in
principle on any fixed finite benchmark; Rung 2 shows that quantifying over all
semantics makes even $95\%$ unattainable.

\emph{Robustness and adversarial evaluation.} The adversarial semantics is a
template for worst-case evaluation, and Rung 2 shows that against a fully
adaptive adversary no fixed deterministic predictor is robust, motivating
restrictions on the adversary in any meaningful guarantee.

\emph{Enumeration and coverage.} Rung 4 is the reason no countable knowledge
base of yes/no behaviours can be complete: some behaviour is always
diagonalized out, independent of resources.

\section{Future work}

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
  \item \textbf{Arithmetic truth as an unbounded limit of bounded tables.} Each
    length-bounded fragment of arithmetic has a finite exact table, yet
    plausibly no single computable procedure produces all of them uniformly.
  \item \textbf{Quantitative advice lower bounds.} Realizing every semantics
    exactly should require $2^n$ bits of advice; under $95\%$ Hamming accuracy,
    optimal advice length should track the volume of radius-$0.05$ Hamming

  \item \textbf{Sound abstention under coverage constraints.} With sound

  \item \textbf{A concrete relativized jump.} A partial-recursive

  \item \textbf{Distribution-sensitive limits.} Under computably samplable

\section{Limits of the present results}

This development does not identify human intuition with a noncomputable
operation, and provides no evidence for that identification. It proves only a
precise finite counterexample, an explicit tabulation, a uniform adversarial
impossibility, finite cardinality formulas, and elementary Cantor-style diagonal
theorems. Connecting mathematical discovery to the computability-theoretic jump
would require a defensible formal model of discovery and a reduction theorem;
neither is supplied here.

\section{Conclusion}

On a bounded language the perfect oracle exists and is a finite table,

    """Enumerate every word of the given length over an `alphabet`-symbol set.

    The number of results is exactly ``alphabet ** length`` (Proposition 2.2).
    """
    return [tuple(w) for w in product(range(alphabet), repeat=length)]


def answer_of_bool(b: bool) -> Answer:
    """Embed a Boolean truth value into a definite answer (the map beta)."""
    return "yes" if b else "no"


def correct(truth: Semantics, oracle: Oracle, x: Statement) -> bool:
    """Correctness counts abstention ("unknown") as failure (Definition 2.5)."""
    return oracle(x) == answer_of_bool(truth(x))


def correct_count(
    truth: Semantics, oracle: Oracle, domain: List[Statement]
) -> int:
    """Number of statements answered correctly on a finite domain."""
    return sum(1 for x in domain if correct(truth, oracle, x))


def meets_benchmark(
    truth: Semantics, oracle: Oracle, domain: List[Statement], pct: int = 95
) -> bool:
    """Integer accuracy test: pct * |domain| <= 100 * correct_count."""
    return pct * len(domain) <= 100 * correct_count(truth, oracle, domain)

# 1 & 2. Perfect finite oracle and its finite table
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def exact_oracle(truth: Semantics) -> Oracle:
    """The exact oracle for a fixed semantics (Definition 3.1)."""
    return lambda x: answer_of_bool(truth(x))


def oracle_table(
    oracle: Oracle, domain: List[Statement]
) -> Dict[Statement, Answer]:
    """The complete finite graph of an oracle (Theorem 3.5)."""
    return {x: oracle(x) for x in domain}

    truth: Semantics = lambda x: (sum(x) % 2 == 1)

    print(f"exact oracle correct count = {c} / {len(domain)} "

    print("first 4 rows of the finite lookup table:")
    for x in domain[:4]:

# 3. No universal oracle: the adversarial semantics
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def adversarial_truth(oracle: Oracle) -> Semantics:
    """Semantics chosen in response to an oracle to falsify it (Definition 4.1)."""
    def tau(x: Statement) -> bool:
        a = oracle(x)
        if a == "yes":

        # oracle said "no" or "unknown" -> make it true
        return True
    return tau

# 4. Diagonal escape (finite and infinite echoes)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def finite_diagonal(rows: List[List[bool]]) -> List[bool]:
    """Complement the diagonal of an n x n Boolean table (Definition 5.1)."""
    n = len(rows)
    return [not rows[i][i] for i in range(n)]


def diagonal_jump(row: Callable[[int, int], bool], k_max: int) -> List[bool]:
    """First k_max entries of the diagonal-complement sequence (Definition 5.4)."""
    return [not row(k, k) for k in range(k_max)]

no predictor works uniformly for every semantics, and no countable table of

abbrev Statement (alphabet length : ℕ) := LibraryOfBabel.Word alphabet length

inductive Answer where

  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- Definite answers embed Boolean truth values. -/
def answerOfBool : Bool → Answer
  | true => .yes
  | false => .no

def Correct {α : Type*} (truth : α → Bool) (oracle : α → Answer) (x : α) : Prop :=

  infer_instance

def correctCount {α : Type*} [Fintype α] (truth : α → Bool) (oracle : α → Answer) : ℕ :=

/-- The exact oracle is correct pointwise. -/
lemma exactOracle_correct {α : Type*} (truth : α → Bool) (x : α) :

  rfl

  unfold correctCount
  rw [Finset.filter_eq_self.mpr]

def adversarialTruth {α : Type*} (oracle : α → Answer) (x : α) : Bool :=
  match oracle x with

theorem finite_boolean_table_not_surjective (n : ℕ)

    ¬ Function.Surjective rows := by
  intro hsurj
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := hsurj (finiteDiagonal rows)
  exact finiteDiagonal_ne_row rows i hi.symm

def diagonalJump (rows : ℕ → ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → Bool :=
  fun k => !(rows k k)

  cases hbit : rows k k <;> simp [hbit] at hk

theorem no_enumeration_of_boolean_sequences (rows : ℕ → (ℕ → Bool)) :

  intro hsurj
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := hsurj (diagonalJump rows)

explicit: there are `alphabet ^ length` encoded statements. -/
theorem bounded_statement_cardinality (alphabet length : ℕ) :
    Fintype.card (Statement alphabet length) = alphabet ^ length := by

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple

# Core model
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Statement = Tuple[int, ...]          # a length-`length` word over {0,...,a-1}
Answer = str                         # "yes" | "no" | "unknown"
Semantics = Callable[[Statement], bool]
Oracle = Callable[[Statement], Answer]


def all_statements(alphabet: int, length: int) -> List[Statement]:
    """Enumerate every word of the given length over an `alphabet`-symbol set.

    The number of results is exactly ``alphabet ** length`` (Proposition 2.2).
    """
    return [tuple(w) for w in product(range(alphabet), repeat=length)]


def answer_of_bool(b: bool) -> Answer:
    """Embed a Boolean truth value into a definite answer (the map beta)."""
    return "yes" if b else "no"


def correct(truth: Semantics, oracle: Oracle, x: Statement) -> bool:
    """Correctness counts abstention ("unknown") as failure (Definition 2.5)."""
    return oracle(x) == answer_of_bool(truth(x))


def correct_count(
    truth: Semantics, oracle: Oracle, domain: List[Statement]
) -> int:
    """Number of statements answered correctly on a finite domain."""
    return sum(1 for x in domain if correct(truth, oracle, x))

) -> bool:

    return pct * len(domain) <= 100 * correct_count(truth, oracle, domain)

concept.concept_description:
# Future directions

This development formalizes the finite coordinate core of Curtin's *Generalizations of nets and Latin squares* (arXiv:2607.10890v1): column- and row-Latin matrices, orthogonality, cooperative pairs and systems, coordinate reticulations, svelte arrays, unique cross-line intersections, the grid-coordinate characterizations of Lemma 7.5, and the `m*n` cardinality consequence of Theorem 3.1.

Natural next steps are:

1. **Partition-level incidence structures.** Connect the coordinate-fibre representation here to a literal structure whose lines are finite sets and whose families are `Set.PairwiseDisjoint` covers. Prove both representations equivalent, including all seven clauses of Theorem 3.1.
2. **Full inverse correspondence.** Package the maps between ordered reticulations, svelte semi-orthogonal arrays, and normalized cooperative systems as equivalences, proving Theorems 6.2, 6.3, 7.7, and 7.8 at structure level rather than only the forward encodings established here.
3. **Multiplicity and foundations.** Model multisets of line families, then formalize repetition-free reticulations and Proposition 4.1.
4. **Parastrophy and isotopy.** Define the permutation actions from Sections 9 and 10 and prove that they preserve the cooperative and reticulation axioms.
5. **Constructions.** Formalize prolongation, splicing, and direct products from Sections 12–14, with formulas for their parameters.
6. **Classical specializations.** Build translations from nets, mixed orthogonal arrays, mutually orthogonal Latin squares, and bireversible Mealy automata, recovering Propositions 3.6 and 6.6 and Theorem 7.3.
7. **Finite search.** Add executable enumeration of small repetition-free systems up to isotopy, together with kernel-checked certificates for any reported counts.

  rcases (adjacency_mul_eq_iff_unique R S U).mp hMPF x z with h | h
  · exact h.2
  · exact (h.1 hxz).elim

/-- A non-edge of the target of an MPF has no factorization through an intermediate
vertex. -/
theorem no_intermediate_of_mpf
    (R S U : V → V → Prop)
    [DecidableRel R] [DecidableRel S] [DecidableRel U]
    (hMPF : adjacency R * adjacency S = adjacency U)
    {x z : V} (hxz : ¬ U x z) :
    ¬ ∃ y, R x y ∧ S y z := by
  rcases (adjacency_mul_eq_iff_unique R S U).mp hMPF x z with h | h
  · exact (hxz h.1).elim
  · exact h.2

/-- The sum of an adjacency-matrix row is its outdegree. -/
lemma adjacency_row_sum (R : V → V → Prop) [DecidableRel R] (x : V) :
    ∑ y, adjacency R x y = outDegree R x := by
  simp only [adjacency, outDegree]
  rw [Finset.card_filter]

/-- Valencies multiply in every MPF.  This is the basic arithmetic obstruction used
throughout the classification theory of association-scheme factorizations. -/
theorem valency_multiplication
    (R S U : V → V → Prop)
    [DecidableRel R] [DecidableRel S] [DecidableRel U] [Nonempty V]
    {r s u : ℕ} (hR : IsRegular R r) (hS : IsRegular S s)
    (hU : IsRegular U u)
    (hMPF : adjacency R * adjacency S = adjacency U) :
    u = r * s := by
  let x : V := Classical.choice (inferInstance : Nonempty V)
  have hrows : (∑ z, (adjacency R * adjacency S) x z) = ∑ z, adjacency U x z := by
    simpa using congrArg (fun M : Matrix V V ℕ => ∑ z, M x z) hMPF
  have hleft : (∑ z, (adjacency R * adjacency S) x z) = r * s := by
    simp only [Matrix.mul_apply]
    rw [Finset.sum_comm]
    simp_rw [← Finset.mul_sum]
    simp_rw [adjacency_row_sum]
    have heq : (∑ y, adjacency R x y * outDegree S y) =
        ∑ y, adjacency R x y * s := by
      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
      intro y hy
      rw [hS y]
    rw [heq, ← Finset.sum_mul, adjacency_row_sum, hR]
  have hright : (∑ z, adjacency U x z) = u := by
    rw [adjacency_row_sum, hU x]
  omega

/-- In the universal-complement case, valencies satisfy `r*s = |V|-1`.  This is the
first numerical restriction behind the universal pentagon theorem. -/
theorem complement_valency_restriction
    (R S : V → V → Prop)
    [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel R] [DecidableRel S] [Nonempty V]
    {r s : ℕ} (hR : IsRegular R r) (hS : IsRegular S s)
    (hMPF : adjacency R * adjacency S = adjacency (fun x y : V => x ≠ y)) :
    r * s = Fintype.card V - 1 := by
  have hreg : IsRegular (fun x y : V => x ≠ y) (Fintype.card V - 1) := by
    intro x
    unfold outDegree
    rw [show (Finset.univ.filter fun y : V => x ≠ y) = Finset.univ.erase x by
      ext y
      simp [ne_comm]]
    rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem (Finset.mem_univ x)]
    simp
  exact (valency_multiplication R S (fun x y : V => x ≠ y)
    hR hS hreg hMPF).symm

/-- Transposing an MPF reverses its factors.  For symmetric relations this says that
an MPF automatically holds in the opposite order, as it does in a commutative symmetric
association scheme. -/
theorem reverse_mpf_of_symmetric
    (R S U : V → V → Prop)
    [DecidableRel R] [DecidableRel S] [DecidableRel U]
    (hR : Symmetric R) (hS : Symmetric S) (hU : Symmetric U)
    (hMPF : adjacency R * adjacency S = adjacency U) :
    adjacency S * adjacency R = adjacency U := by
  funext x z
  rw [adjacency_mul_apply_eq_card]
  have hcount := congrFun (congrFun hMPF z) x
  rw [adjacency_mul_apply_eq_card] at hcount
  rw [show (Finset.univ.filter fun y => S x y ∧ R y z) =
      Finset.univ.filter fun y => R z y ∧ S y x by
    apply Finset.filter_congr
    intro y hy
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hs, hr⟩
      exact ⟨hR hr, hS hs⟩
    · rintro ⟨hr, hs⟩
      exact ⟨hS hs, hR hr⟩]
  rw [hcount]
  unfold adjacency
  by_cases h : U x z
  · simp [h, hU h]
  · have hn : ¬ U z x := fun hzx => h (hU hzx)
    simp [h, hn]

/-!
## The pentagon: the 5-cycle factorization of `J - I`

The headline example of the theory is the scheme of the 5-cycle `C₅`.  Its two nontrivial
basic relations are "distance one" and "distance two", each of valency two, and their
ordinary matrix product is exactly the all-ones-minus-identity matrix `J - I`.  This is a
genuine loopless matrix-product factorization, showing the general criteria above are not
vacuous, and it saturates `complement_valency_restriction` with `2 * 2 = 5 - 1`.
-/

namespace Pentagon

/-- Distance-one relation on the 5-cycle `ℤ/5`. -/
def R1 : Fin 5 → Fin 5 → Prop := fun x y => y = x + 1 ∨ x = y + 1

/-- Distance-two relation on the 5-cycle `ℤ/5`. -/
def R2 : Fin 5 → Fin 5 → Prop := fun x y => y = x + 2 ∨ x = y + 2

instance : DecidableRel R1 := fun x y => by unfold R1; infer_instance
instance : DecidableRel R2 := fun x y => by unfold R2; infer_instance

/-- Both basic relations are symmetric. -/
theorem R1_symmetric : Symmetric R1 := by unfold Symmetric R1; decide
theorem R2_symmetric : Symmetric R2 := by unfold Symmetric R2; decide

/-- The distance-one relation has valency two. -/
theorem R1_regular : IsRegular R1 2 := by unfold IsRegular outDegree; decide

/-- The distance-two relation has valency two. -/
theorem R2_regular : IsRegular R2 2 := by unfold IsRegular outDegree; decide

/-- **The pentagon factorization.**  On the 5-cycle the product of the distance-one and
distance-two adjacency matrices is `J - I`, the adjacency matrix of the "distinct"
relation.  This is a nontrivial loopless MPF. -/
theorem pentagon_mpf :
    adjacency R1 * adjacency R2 = adjacency (fun x y : Fin 5 => x ≠ y) := by decide

/-- The pentagon example realizes the universal-complement valency equation
`r * s = |V| - 1` with `r = s = 2` and `|V| = 5`. -/
theorem pentagon_valency_restriction : (2 : ℕ) * 2 = Fintype.card (Fin 5) - 1 :=
  complement_valency_restriction R1 R2 R1_regular R2_regular pentagon_mpf

/-- Every non-loop pair of the pentagon has a unique distance-one/distance-two witness. -/
theorem pentagon_unique_intermediate {x z : Fin 5} (hxz : x ≠ z) :
    ∃! y, R1 x y ∧ R2 y z :=
  unique_intermediate_of_mpf R1 R2 (fun x y : Fin 5 => x ≠ y) pentagon_mpf hxz

end Pentagon

end AssociationSchemeMPF

# Computational evidence: relation matrix-product factorizations

The formal target is the structural criterion saying that a zero-one matrix product is
a target adjacency matrix exactly when target pairs have one intermediate witness and
non-target pairs have none.

## Small cases

For the cycle `C₅`, label vertices modulo 5 and let `R(x,y)` mean that `y-x = ±1`.
Each ordered pair of distinct vertices has exactly one two-step decomposition in which
both steps are cycle edges: adjacent pairs use the route going the long way by two signed
steps, while distance-two pairs use their common neighbor. Hence the adjacency matrix
satisfies `A_R² = J - I`. Its valency check is `2·2 = 5-1`.

For cycles `Cₙ`, the same product has diagonal entry 2 at every vertex, so `A_R²` itself
cannot be loopless. The `C₅` phenomenon concerns the relevant factor relations as framed
by the unique-witness criterion, and demonstrates why witness multiplicity is decisive.

## Counterexample hunt / boundary checks

* Empty factor: if either relation has no outgoing edges, the product is zero; the
  criterion predicts no witnesses everywhere.
* Complete directed loopless relation on 3 vertices: a diagonal pair has two two-step
  witnesses, so its square is not zero-one. This is correctly rejected.
* A permutation relation has exactly one outgoing edge. Multiplying by it merely relabels
  columns, and every resulting entry remains zero-one; this is the valency-one (trivial)
  family highlighted in Hamming-scheme classifications.

## Sequence/OEIS

No new integer sequence is needed: the numerical consequence is the elementary divisor
constraint `r*s = |V|-1` in the universal-complement case, rather than a sequence claim.
Accordingly no OEIS search was relevant.

## Table

| vertices | factor valencies `(r,s)` allowed by `r*s=n-1` |
|---:|:---|
| 3 | `(1,2)`, `(2,1)` |
| 4 | `(1,3)`, `(3,1)` |
| 5 | `(1,4)`, `(2,2)`, `(4,1)` |

# Future directions

1. **Universal pentagon theorem.** The concrete 5-cycle instance is now formalized in
   `Core.lean` (`Pentagon.pentagon_mpf`, `Pentagon.pentagon_valency_restriction`), giving
   an explicit nontrivial factorization `A₁ A₂ = J - I` with `2 * 2 = 5 - 1`. The

   loopless, symmetric, association-scheme intersection-number hypotheses and prove that
   any nontrivial factorization of `J-I` forces five vertices and two valency-two factors.
2. **Spectral criterion.** Develop the simultaneous diagonalization of the Bose–Mesner
   algebra and prove the coordinatewise eigenvalue criterion
   `theta_S(j) * theta_T(j) = theta_U(j)`.
3. **Rank obstruction.** Combine the spectral criterion with rank inequalities for
   matrix products. Formalize the extremal equality case in which every nonzero target
   eigenvalue is `±k(U)`, and connect this to bipartiteness.
4. **Two-class classification.** Encode strongly regular graph parameters and derive the
   parameter equations imposed by an MPF, culminating in the `C₅` classification.
5. **P-polynomial schemes.** Formalize the distance-regular three-term recurrence for
   `A₁ Aᵢ` and classify when all coefficients are zero or one with loopless support.

   intersection-number formula, and formalize the binary identity
   `A₁ A_d = A_{d-1}` together with the nonexistence result for `q > 2`.
7. **Rectangular and directed extensions.** The unique-witness criterion in `Core.lean`
   does not require symmetry. It can support analogous results for coherent
   configurations, directed relations, and incidence matrices of finite geometries.
